title: Janaka's court: the thousand cows with gold horns (3.1)
hook: a king offers a thousand gold-horned cows to the wisest person in the room, and only one man dares to take them
tomorrow: Ashvala asks about death and ritual

segments.voice: Yesterday, the honey doctrine: the earth is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for the earth. Your line was madhu. Were you honey for someone, small enough they didn't notice? Day three hundred seventy-one.

A royal courtyard, crowded with learned priests from the Kuru and Panchala lands. In the middle, penned together, a thousand cows. On the horns of every one, the text says, gold is tied. King Janaka stands up. Honored scholars, he says, whoever among you is wisest in Brahman, drive these cows home. And the room goes silent. Nobody moves. Taking the cows means claiming to be the wisest person there. Stand up, and every other priest there will come for you.
screen: `A THOUSAND COWS. GOLD ON THEIR HORNS.` → `WHOEVER IS WISEST, TAKE THEM.` → `NOBODY MOVES.`

segments.voice: Then Yajnavalkya turns to his own student. Samashravas, my dear, he says, drive them home. And the student does. The room explodes. How can he call himself the wisest among us? The king's own hotri priest, Ashvala, steps up. Yajnavalkya, are you really the wisest among us? And Yajnavalkya answers. We bow to the wisest. We just want the cows. It's funny, and it's sly. He doesn't claim anything. He just wants the cows, and he'll answer any question you've got. That sets up the whole third book of the Brihadaranyaka: a day of debate. One after another, challengers step forward, one of them twice, and each asks the hardest question they have. Over the next ten days we'll take them one at a time. And a word about the king. Janaka of Videha appears again and again in these texts as a king hungry for teaching. Sita's father in the Ramayana is also called Janaka, king of Videha. Janaka may have been a name several kings of Videha carried, and nobody can say for sure whether these are the same man. Look back at this week. The self is dearer than a son. The man who left. Maitreyi set aside the earth. Seen, heard, reflected on. Salt with no inside or outside. Honey for each other. And now a room full of cows, and a question that could cost someone everything.
screen: `DRIVE THEM HOME, MY DEAR.` · `WE BOW TO THE WISEST.` · `WE JUST WANT THE COWS.` · `CHALLENGERS, ONE AT A TIME.` · then, large: `WHO IS THE WISEST?`

segments.voice: Two minutes in the silent courtyard. Sit, and breathe. If a memory comes, recall a time you stayed quiet in a room because speaking up meant being judged. A meeting, a class, a family dinner. Don't relive it; just notice how it felt in the body. Then bring to mind Yajnavalkya's ease: no claim to be wisest, just we bow to the wisest. Let some of that ease into your shoulders. Rest there with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Janaka's court. Where a king asked for the brahmishtha, the one most wise in Brahman: the title nobody there dared to claim, and Yajnavalkya never quite claimed either.
Your line: who is the wisest? Today, when someone asks you a question you can answer, answer it, without first proving you're the one who should. Day three hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: The debate in Janaka's court, the third book of the Brihadaranyaka, is studied in Vedanta as a series of short dialogues; Hindu tradition remembers Janaka as a model of the king who lives among riches without clinging to them.

fork.setup: you're Yajnavalkya. the king offers a thousand gold-horned cows to the wisest, and the whole room is silent. what do you do?
options: tell your student to drive the cows home.
give a speech proving you're the wisest.
fork.reveal: he quietly tells his student to drive them home. when challenged, he doesn't argue: we bow to the wisest; we just want the cows.

original.note: Sanskrit brahmiṣṭha: most knowing of Brahman, the superlative Janaka used for the prize.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a contest for cows.
what it means: a king's challenge that opens a whole day of the hardest questions in the Upanishads.
what a scholar hears: Yajnavalkya never claims to be brahmiṣṭha; namo vayaṃ brahmiṣṭhāya kurmaḥ, we bow to the wisest (3.1.2). the challengers follow one by one through 3.9, Gargi twice.

notes: Gold on the horns: the text says ten pādas of gold were tied to each cow's horns; the script says only 'gold is tied'. Confirm.
Challengers counted as eight (Ashvala, Artabhaga, Bhujyu, Ushasta, Kahola, Gargi twice, Uddalaka, Shakalya). Confirm the count fits how the path presents it.
'Over the next ten days': days 372–381 cover the challengers. Adjust if the outline changes.
Janaka of the Upanishads and Sita's father: the script says nobody can say for sure they are the same; Hindu tradition sometimes identifies them. Confirm the phrasing.
